Exercises¶

E3.30¶

Run the $z$-test for the mean of the kombucha volume measurements from Batch 05 to determine if it is a regular batch or not.

a) Formulate two competing hypotheses $H_0$ and $H_A$.

b) Calculate the sample mean $\overline{\mathbf{k}}_{05}$.

c) Find the sampling distribution of the mean $\overline{\mathbf{K}}_0$ under the population data model $K_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{K_0}\!=\!1000, \sigma_{K_0}\!=\!10)$. Use the formula $\stderr{\overline{\mathbf{k}}} = \frac{\sigma_{K_0}}{\sqrt{n}}$ to get the standard error of the mean.

d) Compute the two-sided $p$-value of the observed $\overline{\mathbf{k}}_{05}$ under $\overline{\mathbf{K}}_0$.

e) Make a decision about Batch 05 using the cutoff value $\alpha\!=\!0.05$.

E3.31¶

Run a $z$-test for the mean $\mu$ of kombucha Batch 06. Compute a two-sided $p$-value using two methods:

a) Compute the $z$-statistic $z = \frac{\overline{\mathbf{k}}_{06} - \mu_{K_0}}{\stderr{\overline{\mathbf{k}}}}$, where $\stderr{\overline{\mathbf{k}}} = \frac{\sigma_{K_0}}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the standard error of the mean, then compute the $p$-value using the standard normal $Z_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ as the reference distribution.

b) Compute the $p$-value directly from $\overline{\mathbf{k}}_{06}$ and the normal model for the sampling distribution of the mean $\overline{\mathbf{K}}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{K_0}, \stderr{\overline{\mathbf{k}}})$.

Make a decision by comparing the $p$-value to the cutoff $\alpha\!=\!0.05$.

E3.32¶

Run the two-sided $t$-test for the mean on Batch 05 of the kombucha dataset to determine if it is a regular batch or not.

a) Formulate the two competing hypotheses $H_0$ and $H_A$. Specify, in full detail, the data models under the two hypotheses and all assumptions about the model parameters you're making.

b) Calculate the mean $\overline{\mathbf{k}}_{05}$ and the standard deviation $s_{\mathbf{k}_{05}}$.

c) Calculate the estimated standard error using $\stderrhat{\overline{\mathbf{k}}} = \frac{ s_{\mathbf{k}_{05}} }{\sqrt{n}}$.

d) Compute the $t$-statistic using the formula $t = \frac{\overline{\mathbf{k}}_{05} - \mu_{K_0}}{\stderrhat{\overline{\mathbf{k}}}}$.

e) Compute the two-sided $p$-value of the $t$-statistic under the standard $t$-distribution with $\nu = n-1$ degrees of freedom.

f) Repeat the $p$-value calculation by computing the probability of observing a deviation of $\overline{\mathbf{k}}_{05}$ or larger under the model $T_{\overline{\mathbf{K}}_0} \sim \mathcal{T}(n-1, \mu_{K_0}, \stderrhat{\overline{\mathbf{k}}})$ for the sampling distribution of the mean.

g) Make a decision about Batch 05 using the cutoff value $\alpha\!=\!0.05$.

The $p$-value is less than $\alpha = 0.05$ so we reject $H_0$. Batch 05 seems to be irregular.

Note we previously reached a different conclusion after the analysis of the data from Batch 05 using the $z$-test. The difference is that in we assumed $\sigma_{K_0}=10$, whereas in the current analysis we estimated the standard deviation from the sample.

E3.33¶

Run a two-sided $t$-test for the mean of kombucha Batch 06.

a) Compute a two-sided $p$-value of $\overline{\mathbf{k}}_{06}$ under the sampling distribution of the mean $\overline{\mathbf{K}}_0 \approx T_{\overline{\mathbf{K}}_0} \sim \mathcal{T}(\nu,\mu_{K_0}, \frac{ s_{\mathbf{k}_{06}} }{\sqrt{n}})$, with $\nu = n-1$.

b) Make a decision by comparing the $p$-value to the cutoff $\alpha\!=\!0.05$.

c) Compute a point estimate $\hat{\Delta}$ for the effect size $\Delta = \mu_{06} - \mu_{K_0}$ and a $90\%$ confidence interval for the effect size $\ci{\Delta,0.9}$.

Hint: Use the function ci_mean with the option method="a" to obtain a confidence interval for $\mu_{06}$ based on Student's $t$-distribution.

E3.36 Drug discovery¶

The baseline model for the health indicator of people who have an ailment is $I_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{I_0}\!=\!100, \sigma_{I_0})$. A group of $10$ patients are treated with a new drug, and their health indicator measurements after the treatment are recorded. The observed data is $\mathbf{i} = (101.9, 100.4, 99.9, 100.4, 101.1, 100.8, 100.8, 101.2, 99.8, 102.5)$. You want to know if the new drug has an effect on the health indicator so you run a hypothesis test based on the hypotheses $H_A: \mu \neq \mu_{I_0}$ and $H_0: \mu = \mu_{I_0}$. E3.38¶

Explain in your own words what is wrong with the following interpretations of $p$-values:

a) A small $p$-value like $p=0.02$ proves that $H_A$ is true.

b) The $p$-value = $0.02$ obtained in a clinical trial of a new drug (compared to no treatment) proves that the new drug works.

c) A large $p$-value like $p=0.4$ proves that $H_0$ is true.

d) The $p$-value $0.02$ tells us the probability that $H_0$ is true is 2%.

e) The $p$-value $0.02$ tells us the probability that $H_A$ is true is 98%.

f) When the $p$-value is $0.02$ and we decide to reject $H_0$, there is only a 2% probability that we made a wrong decision.

g) The $p$-value of $0.02$ tells us that there is a 98% probability that a replication of the experiment will also reject $H_0$.

h) The tiny $p$-value $0.002$ obtained in a clinical test of a new medication means the medication is very effective.

Hint: Recall the probability calculations used to compute $p$-values.

A small $p$-value counts as evidence against $H_0$, but it is wrong to claim that we have proved or definitely shown that the null hypothesis is false. Conversely, a large $p$-value means the observed data are not particularly surprising under $H_0$, but it does not prove that $H_0$ is true. The logic of hypothesis testing is probabilistic and not absolute: this is why the strong statements in a), b), and c) are all wrong.

The $p$-value we compute as part of a hypothesis test is the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained from the observed data, assuming that the null hypothesis is true. Informally, we can write this as $p = \textrm{Pr}(\textbf{data}|H_0)$. The $p$-value calculation doesn't calculate the probability of the hypotheses given the data $\textrm{Pr}(H_0|\textbf{data})$, so the statement d) is incorrect. Similarly, knowing the $p$-value doesn't give us $\textrm{Pr}(H_A|\textbf{data})$, so e) is also a wrong interpretation. In fact, the data model under $H_A$ did not enter at all into the $p$-value calculation! In general, any statement about the "probability of" $H_0$ or $H_A$ is not going to be correct.

The $p$-value is not the probability that we made a mistake, so f) is false. In a particular hypothesis test where we reject $H_0$, we either made a mistake or not, similar to how a particular confidence interval either correctly captures the unknown parameter or doesn't. The cutoff value $\alpha$ we use to make our decision is related to the probability of falsely rejecting $H_0$ across repeated samples, but that doesn't tell us anything about any particular analysis.

Interpretation g) seems to confuse $(1-p)$ with a probability of replication. The $p$-value is not an indication of the magnitude of the effect, so h) is false. In a large sample, it is possible to obtain a tiny $p$-value (highly significant result) when testing a drug that has a negligible effect on health.
